paragraphs: A new study looked at poor children in Ireland. It found that many of them do not like school.
About half of Irish children are poor at some time before age 13. One in five are poor three times or more.
Poor children have fewer books at home. Their parents often have less time to read to them. They also do fewer sports and arts activities.
At age nine, 9% of poor children never like school. For other children, it is 4%. At 13, most children want to go to university. But only 62% of poor children do.
The study says schools can help. It wants money for sports and arts for all children.

A new study by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) shows that children who grow up in poverty are more than twice as likely to dislike school. One important reason is that they do not have enough books.
The study found that about half of Irish children were poor at some point before the age of 13, and one in five were poor three or more times. Each time a child was poor, their reading got worse.

Poor children often have fewer books at home, and their parents spend less time reading to them. They also take part in fewer sports and cultural activities. At age nine, 9% of these children never like school, compared with 4% of other children. At 13, 79% of all children expect to get a degree, but only 62% of poor children do.

The ESRI wants the Government to pay for sports and arts so every child can join in. Emer Smyth, one of the authors, said good relationships between teachers and students are very important. Children's Minister Norma Foley said the study shows why fighting child poverty matters.

Children who experience persistent poverty are more than twice as likely to dislike school as those who have never been poor, according to new research from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI). The report, funded by the Department of Children, identifies limited access to books as a key factor.

Roughly half of Irish children experienced poverty at some stage before turning 13, while one in five went through three or more spells. Each period of poverty was linked to a drop in reading ability.

The researchers found that poorer families tend to own fewer books, read less to their children by the age of five and do fewer learning activities at home. These children are also less likely to take part in sport and cultural activities. At nine, 9% of persistently poor children said they never liked school, compared with 4% of those never in poverty. By 13, 79% of children expected to earn a degree, falling to 62% among the persistently poor.

The ESRI is calling for subsidies so that all children can access sport and the arts, and for positive school environments. Co-author Emer Smyth said school climate was key, while Minister Norma Foley said the findings underlined the need to tackle child poverty.

Children growing up in persistent poverty are more than twice as likely to be disaffected with school as their better-off peers, a new Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) study has found, pinpointing a scarcity of books as a major culprit.

Earlier research had established a link between childhood deprivation and weaker educational outcomes without fully explaining it. The report sheds light on this: around half of Irish children endured poverty at some point before 13, and one in five suffered three or more bouts, each of which coincided with a dip in reading attainment.

Deprived households typically have fewer books, devote less time to reading aloud to young children and engage in fewer stimulating home activities. Such children are also largely excluded from sport and culture. At nine, 9% of persistently poor children professed never to like school, double the rate among those spared poverty, and aspirations lag too: 62% expect to earn a degree, against 79% overall.

The authors urge subsidised access to extracurricular pursuits and a nurturing school climate. Research professor Emer Smyth stressed the pivotal role of teacher-student relationships, while Minister Norma Foley said the findings reinforced the imperative of tackling child poverty.

According to a recent study by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI), children who experience persistent poverty are more than twice as likely to hold negative attitudes towards school as those who have never been poor. The report identifies insufficient access to books as a significant contributing factor.

Although previous research had demonstrated a correlation between childhood poverty and poorer educational outcomes, the underlying mechanisms had remained unclear. The study indicates that approximately half of Irish children experienced poverty before the age of 13, and that each episode was associated with a decline in reading proficiency.

Several factors appear to account for this pattern, including limited access to books, less frequent shared reading and reduced participation in cultural and sporting activities. Consequently, 9% of persistently poor nine-year-olds reported never enjoying school, compared with 4% of their peers, while only 62% anticipated obtaining a degree, as opposed to 79% of all 13-year-olds.

The authors therefore recommend subsidies to ensure equitable access to extracurricular activities, alongside supportive school environments. Nevertheless, as the Minister for Children, Norma Foley, acknowledged, sustained progress is ultimately contingent upon tackling child poverty itself.
